chunks: From him, from a number of our companions, from Sahl ibn Ziyad, from Mansur ibn al-Abbas, from Ibrahim al-Ahwal, from Imran al-Za'faranī, who said:

I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): 'We stay in winter for the day and the two days, we do not see the sun or the moon (crescent). On which day should we fast?' He said: 'Look at the day you fasted from the past year, count five days, and fast the fifth day.'

So in these two reports, the ruling within them is that if the sky is cloudy regarding what they contained, it is upon the person to fast the fifth day from the fasting of the day of the past year, assuming it is from Sha'ban; if his counting of its deficiency is not established, he acts cautiously. If it happens to be from the month of Ramadan, it has sufficed for him, and if it is from Sha'ban, it is recorded for him as supererogatory. This runs the course of fasting the Day of Doubt, and the report does not state that he fasts the fifth day assuming it is from Ramadan. And if this is not in its apparent meaning and it bears what we said, the objection against it falls away, and it does not contradict what we mentioned of acting upon the crescents.

key_terms.صِيَامُ يَوْمِ الشَّكِّ: Fasting of the Day of Doubt

ai.seo_question: How to determine the start of Ramadan fasting when the moon is not visible in winter?
ai.summary: This narration from Imam al-Sadiq (AS) establishes a practical astronomical calculation (taqwim) for determining the start of Ramadan in high-latitude regions where the crescent may remain hidden for days. The commentary highlights the juristic flexibility of this method, noting that fasting on the calculated day serves as a precautionary act (ihtiyat) that is valid whether it coincides with Ramadan or Sha'ban, thereby avoiding the penalty of fasting on the 'Day of Doubt'.
